s-wh3_saq1-high-0.essay:
(A) One feature of how the London scholars organized their study is that they met regularly, once a week, in places like Goddard's house on Wood Street, the Bull's Head Tavern in Cheapside, and Gresham College. They did not work only inside a university. They also brought together people with different specialties, like the mathematician Wallis and several physicians, so they could share ideas across fields, and members like Goddard actually carried out experiments for the group.

(B) One development that helps explain why these scholars started meeting is Francis Bacon's call in the early 1600s for a new method based on observation and experiment, especially in works like Novum Organum (1620). Bacon argued that knowledge of nature should come from collecting evidence and testing it, not just from reading ancient authorities like Aristotle. Since that kind of inquiry needed many observations and experiments, it made sense for scholars to gather in groups where they could do experiments together and compare results.

(C) One difference is that the English group started as an informal private gathering of gentlemen and later became the Royal Society, while in France the Academy of Sciences, founded in 1666, was set up and paid for by the royal government under Louis XIV and his minister Colbert. French academicians got salaries from the crown and were expected to work on projects useful to the state. The English society got a royal charter but mostly depended on its own members and their money, so it had more independence but less funding.

So it was an informal group that gathered in private homes and public spots instead of in one official building.

(B) One development that helps explain why scholars started meeting is Francis Bacon's call for organized experimental science in the early 1600s. Bacon argued in works like the Novum Organum that knowledge about nature should come from experiments and observation instead of just relying on ancient authorities like Aristotle, and that many people should work on it together. Because of this idea, scholars in England saw that working in a group where they could share results and try experiments together was a better way to learn about nature, which is why groups of natural philosophers began meeting regularly in London.

(C) In France there was the French Academy of Sciences which was started in 1666 during the reign of Louis XIV. It was a scientific organization in France that had scientists working in Paris and it was also an important place for science in Europe in the 1600s. Many famous scholars were part of it and they did experiments and studied nature there.

s-wh3_saq2-high-0.essay:
(A) Taylor claims that the main goal of management should be "maximum prosperity" for both the employer and each employee at once. He argues that for workers this means not just higher wages but being trained to their highest efficiency and given the best grade of work they are fit for, so the two sides' interests could become identical instead of being organized "for war."

(B) The Ford Motor Company's five-dollar day, introduced in 1914, partly supports Taylor's claim. After Ford adopted the moving assembly line at Highland Park in 1913, turnover was very high because the work was monotonous, so Ford roughly doubled the usual daily wage. This lowered turnover and raised productivity for the company, and workers earned much more, so both sides seemed to gain from efficient production the way Taylor predicted. However, Ford's workers still had little control over the pace of the line, which shows the interests were not completely identical.

(C) In Soviet Russia, Lenin publicly endorsed the Taylor system in 1918, arguing that the Soviet state should adopt its scientific methods of organizing labor while rejecting its capitalist exploitation. Later, during Stalin's Five-Year Plans, the state adapted these ideas to push for higher output through the Stakhanovite movement, which began in 1935 when the miner Alexei Stakhanov was celebrated for far exceeding his coal quota. This shows that the Soviets used efficiency methods to serve state industrialization goals rather than private profit.

annotations.comment: Adds accurate detail tying the claim to the excerpt's 'war rather than peace' line.

s-wh3_saq2-mid-0.essay:
(A) Taylor claims that the best goal for management is to get the maximum prosperity for the employer and the maximum prosperity for each employee at the same time. He says that for workers this means higher wages than usual and also being trained to do the best kind of work that fits their abilities, so the employer and the worker do not have to be enemies.

(B) During this time period there were a lot of problems between workers and bosses in factories, and this challenges what Taylor said. Many workers did not like the new methods and thought the bosses only cared about making more money. This shows that the interests of employers and employees were not really identical like Taylor thought, because both sides were still fighting with each other.

(C) One way scientific management was adopted outside the United States was in the Soviet Union. Lenin supported the Taylor system in 1918 because the new Soviet government wanted to build up industry quickly after the revolution. Later, under Stalin's Five-Year Plans starting in 1928, the Soviets used American-style mass production methods in their factories, and the Soviet Union even worked with the Ford Motor Company to build an auto plant at Nizhny Novgorod. This shows the Soviets adapted capitalist production methods to fit their communist goals of fast industrialization.

s-wh3_saq3-high-0.essay:
(A) The print shows people as small and helpless next to nature. The huge wave with claw-like foam curls over three narrow boats, and the rowers are crouched low in them as if they are just holding on. Even Mount Fuji looks tiny in the background, so the overall message is that nature is far more powerful than the humans in it.

(B) During the Tokugawa period, cities like Edo grew very large, and a wealthy class of merchants and townspeople (chonin) developed because of commercial growth during the long peace. These townspeople had money and leisure to spend on entertainment and art, so commercial publishers could print many cheap copies of prints like Hokusai's using carved woodblocks and sell them to a big urban market. This demand from the merchant class is a big reason why ukiyo-e prints were mass produced and sold widely.

(C) After Commodore Perry arrived in 1853 and Japan signed treaties opening its ports, cultural exchange became much more open in both directions. Japanese prints were exported to Europe and became popular with collectors, starting a fashion called Japonisme, and artists like Vincent van Gogh collected and copied ukiyo-e prints. At the same time, the Meiji government sent officials abroad and brought in Western education, technology, and art styles, so exchange moved from the limited Dutch trade at Nagasaki to wide, two-way contact.
